cells.tense: You're still following what you set out after, and you know it's still worth following.
cells.ask: offer it forward one more time this week than you already do — the care that keeps its shape while it holds.
cells.core:
You've stayed with this a long time and it hasn't worn you down. What you hand people has been through things and it's still standing, and that's why it holds weight for them. There's a next edge to it, though: the strength you've proven can be spent on something you haven't chosen yet, or handed to someone who'll keep it going longer than you will.

Holding without forcing is what keeps your hand steady when things get heavy. Not shaping what you carry to fit, just not dropping it. That's the part of you that says what gets passed on can outlast the pressure it's under — and you can let one more thing ride on that than you'd usually risk.
cells.sheetLine: You've kept this alive through everything, and you own the keeping.
cells.verb: keep hoping past the point where hoping plainly works
cells.place: in what gets handed down and kept alive between people

cells.tense: You're bracing for something down the road that hasn't happened yet.
cells.ask: let one thing you're holding go unsaid until you actually know it — knowing that holds its ground before it speaks.
cells.core:
You're holding on so hard the holding has taken over from the thing you're holding. Every new doubt gets met with more effort, more insistence, more trying to prove it'll hold — and the proving is eating the thing it's supposed to protect. What you carry is sturdy; the grip around it isn't trusting that.

Where this is sound, the keeping shines because the thing it carried actually grew, not because you outmuscled the doubt. Reflection is what lets you sit with not knowing for a minute and still trust your read. Let one thing you're carrying sit unanswered until you actually know it. A steady voice comes back instead of a strained one.
cells.sheetLine: You're gripping the thing you're holding so hard it's starting to feel like force.

cells.tense: You're standing at a door you already walked through, still holding the handle.
cells.ask: tend one shared thing — a practice, a promise, a small carrying-forward — without clutching it, and let it grow at its own pace.
cells.core:
You're the one who keeps a small thing alive — a weekly call, a recipe, the way a group greets each other — and it grows because you kept showing up to it. Lately that's gone quiet. You've stopped handing things forward. The strength to keep going is still in you, but it's got nowhere to land, so it's stopped moving. The people who'd carry what you know feel further off than they used to.

Tending something with responsible care is what restores a stretch like this — not pushing harder at what's already still, but looking after one specific thing that grows because you're answerable for it. Keep that promise, show up to the thing that needs showing up to. Care that doesn't exhaust comes back, and it comes back full.
cells.sheetLine: You have something worth carrying forward and you've handed it off to no one.

cells.tense: You're already shaping what people pass around, and you're talking about it as if it were doing it by itself.
cells.ask: claim one thing you keep doing as yours — the plain strength of staying with what's hard — not the tradition's, not the group's, yours.
cells.core:
What keeps going and what gets let go, that's already in your hands — in how you talk about what matters, in what you keep telling people, in what you let slide. That steering is happening now. The way you tell it, though, sounds like the shape of things, or the way it's always been done around here, not like a choice someone's making.

Staying with what's hard because you decided to is the smaller, plainer version of what you're already doing. Not the big story about what this tradition stands for — your own weight on it. Say so about one thing, in the smallest way, and the tradition stops carrying you and starts being yours.
